newsitem.title: USA: Ultrasound detects hard-to-find breast cancers.
newsitem.headline: Ultrasound detects hard-to-find breast cancers.

text.p: Ultrasound examinations can detect breast cancer in some women whose dense breasts camouflage the tumours from mammography X-rays, according to a study released on Monday.

Other researchers on breast cancer detection meanwhile reported that mammograms may benefit women younger than current U.S. government guidelines specify, and that a new technique for breast biopsies may be more accurate and less invasive.

The ultrasound report came from New York radiologist Thomas Kolb, who told the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America that mammography misses about 15 percent of cancers in women with dense breasts.

Women with denser breasts generally have a higher proportion of milk-producing glands relative to fatty tissue inside the breast. Some older postmenopausal women undergoing hormone replacement therapy also develop dense breasts.

"In our study, physician-performed, high-resolution breast ultrasound detected 10 cancers that were missed by mammography in a group of 2,600 women with dense breasts, and detected them at a size and stage comparable to cancers detected by mammography," he said.

Of 8,323 women in the study who underwent a mammography exam, 2,600 were identified as having dense breasts and were given an ultrasound exam in which echoes from high-frequency sound waves form an internal picture. The ultrasound exams found breast masses in 195 patients whose growths were undetected by X-rays, 10 of which turned out to be cancerous.

"My personal feeling is that all women with dense breasts can benefit from ultrasound," Kolb said. "However, we must look at all the risks and benefits, including costs and long-term effects on survival before recommending implementation of widespread ultrasound screening for women with dense breasts."
A typical breast ultrasound exam costs about $150.
In other studies released at the meeting:

-- A radiologist at California's Palo Alto Medical Clinic said a year-old technique for taking samples of a woman's breast tissue to test for cancer was found to be more accurate and less invasive than the common methods currently employed.
The breast biopsy technique, called mammotomy, extracts breast tissue through a small probe equipped with a high-speed rotating cutter and a vacuum, radiologist Roger Jackman said.

-- Swedish researchers said a study of 57,000 women in that country supports the routine use of mammograms to detect breast cancer in women aged 40 to 49 -- younger than approved by current U.S. government guidelines.

Use of the low-dose X-ray technique for women in that age group has been debated since 1993, when the U.S. National Cancer Institute changed its guidelines. The institute said data did not support the routine use of mammograms before age 50 except for women with a family history of breast cancer.

Erik Thurfjell of University Hospital in Uppsala, Sweden, and colleagues said a study of the women, aged 40 to 74 who were given mammograms from 1988 to 1995, supports use of the technique for younger women.
